description: Hi! We’re a team from Military General Secondary School of Information Technology (WOLI), Poland.
summary:
FireCal turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into a burning activity calendar for any place on Earth. NASA FIRMS records fires from five sensors: MODIS on Terra and Aqua since 2000, and VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Their counts are not comparable. VIIRS's 375 m pixels catch about three times more fires than MODIS's 1 km ones, and a sensor outage looks exactly like a quiet day.

FireCal harmonizes them with a machine-learning transfer model into one consistent daily record (daily correlation 0.93 with real VIIRS counts on held-out years in Portugal). It then shows when an area normally burns and how every day, month and year compares. It ranks the episodes that were unusual and looks ahead: a 14-day fire forecast for every grid cell with fire weather, a seasonal outlook, a wind map, and the possible spread of fires burning right now.

Pick a country, a region or any place by name, or draw a box; the app does the rest with free public data. It helps fire services prepare for the season, helps land managers plan burning and protection, and gives scientists a consistent quarter-century record of fire.
details:
Fire leaves a fingerprint in space. Every day, NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments catch the heat of fires all over the planet, and NASA FIRMS has kept every detection since November 2000. It is a priceless record, but not one you can simply plot. Five sensors with different eyes have watched over 25 years, satellites drift and go offline, and raw MODIS undercounts fires by about 63% compared with VIIRS. FireCal turns that patchwork into one consistent burning calendar for any place on Earth, and then looks ahead.

What it does. Pick a country, a province, a geographic region (Iberian Peninsula, Amazon basin, Sahel…), any place by name, or draw a box. FireCal downloads only the data that area needs and builds:

  • A calendar: every day since 2000 as a year × day heat map, raw or against normal, plus a month-by-month view.
  • The normal pattern: when each fire season started, peaked and ended, and the critical periods (the fewest days that hold half and 80% of a normal year's fire). In Poland, for example, 27% of a year's fire happens in just 39 spring days.
  • Unusual episodes: runs of days far above normal for the time of year, ranked.
  • Any month on the map: what burned where and how it compares with normal. For example, August 2025 in Portugal had 3.2× its normal fire, the second-worst August in 25 years. For coming months, it shows what to expect.
  • Forecasts:
    • the chance of fire in every grid cell 1–14 days ahead;
    • area totals with 80% ranges;
    • the Fire Weather Index and the chance of a critical day;
    • a 1–3 month outlook;
    • a backtest from any past date.
  • Wind and spread:
    • an animated 16-day wind map;
    • the fires burning right now;
    • a simulation of where each fire could be in 1–3 days;
    • an alert when a fire could reach built-up land.

How it works.

  1. Clean data. Low-confidence detections, volcanoes, factories and gas flares are removed. Sensor outages are detected, so "no data" is never read as "no fire".
  2. Harmonization. A LightGBM model trained on the years both instruments flew (2012–2020) translates MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent detections, cell by cell and day by day. A quantile mapping keeps realistic quiet days, so the 2000s look like the 2020s in the calendar.
  3. Calendar statistics on that one record. The fire year starts at the quietest month, so southern seasons that cross New Year stay whole.
  4. Forecast. Two LightGBM models per cell and day, fed with:
    • recent fire seen by all satellites;
    • NASA POWER (MERRA-2) weather for training and Open-Meteo forecasts in operation;
    • the Canadian Fire Weather Index system, drought and snow;
    • fire carried by the wind from burning neighbours;
    • fuel memory and El Niño.
  5. Spread. For each active fire, the Canadian Fire Behaviour Prediction system runs on a grid built from:
    The fire front's travel time comes from Dijkstra's algorithm, so the simulated fire runs downwind and uphill and goes around lakes and villages.
    • NASA MODIS land cover (via GIBS);
    • 10 m Sentinel-2 land cover, where water and towns don't burn;
    • terrain slope;
    • drought;
    • hourly wind.

How well it works (measured only on data the models never saw):

  • MODIS → VIIRS: daily correlation 0.93 with real VIIRS counts in Portugal and the Paraná Delta.
  • 14-day forecast on 2024–2025:
    • cell AUC 0.84–0.88 versus 0.75–0.83 for the climatological normal;
    • it cuts the typical error of daily area totals by 29–38% against the normal;
    • these scores use observed weather, so they are an upper bound; the app also reports the lower bound with no weather forecast.

Benefits and impact.

  • Fire services see when their season starts and spot an unusual year early.
  • Land managers plan prescribed burning and protection around critical periods.
  • Scientists get one consistent quarter-century record instead of five incompatible ones.
  • Communities can check what is burning near them and where the wind is pushing it.

No account, no license and no special hardware are needed: free public data, open-source code, one command on any laptop.

What makes it creative.

  • It makes two generations of satellites comparable.
  • It separates the expected value (right for totals) from the most likely day (right for a single day).
  • It reports its own skill honestly, including where it has none.
  • It joins the calendar, the forecast and live fires on one map: a timeline slides through months and years, wind flows across the area, and simulated fires route around towns.

What we considered.

  • "No data" is not "no fire".
  • Satellite orbit drift.
  • Small fires MODIS cannot see.
  • Seasons that cross New Year.
  • Industrial heat sources.
  • Fair testing on unseen years only.
  • Readability for non-experts: a one-sentence summary, and everything about a place on hover.
  • Accessibility: dark mode, keyboard, phones.
  • Using only free, keyless data, so anyone in the world can run it.

Tools.

  • Python: NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, Shapely, PyArrow, FastAPI, Pillow.
  • JavaScript with Leaflet and hand-made SVG/canvas charts; HTML/CSS.
  • uv, pytest, Playwright, Git/GitHub.
  • Claude Code (AI coding assistant).
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops.
